comment: The 68/300 were scored by the older access-keyed SpecLFB checker: every one of the 68 transmitters read the pre-warmed line 0x3580 and hit in the dcache. SpecLFB scopes speculative hits out, and SimSpect's own current SpecLFB criteria (install-keyed check_ld_speclfb, speclfb.json fill/evict) do not count them; the four hits re-checked after the re-key all flipped to not-a-leak.
proposed: SpecLFB leaves a conditional unsafe speculative load unprotected (isUnsafe=0), which then accesses the cache in-window on [N] tests; under SpecLFB's own criterion (an L1D/L2 fill by an unsafe load) [N] tests leak.
evidence: SpecLFB §9 p643 ('Leakage through speculative loads under cache hits is out of the current defense scope'); simspect wiki/results/PAPER_RESULTS.md:302-304; claudelog 2026-06-03 'CHECKER CHANGE'; STAGE3_gem5/check_ld_speclfb.py:20-34; specs/leakage/speclfb.json

comment: Test #6 and the 23% density come from the same superseded access-keyed criterion that counted cache hits, so they do not measure SpecLFB leaks under its own scope; AMuLeT's #39 is a real CT-SEQ violation, so the comparison is not like for like.
proposed: Re-measure first detection and density under the install/fill criterion (specs/leakage/speclfb.json), or drop the comparison until then.
evidence: PAPER_RESULTS.md §4 and :485-490; claudelog 2026-06-03 (both entries); SpecLFB §9 p643

anchor: reproducing SpecLFB's known unprotected-first-load bug with far fewer tests than prior work.
comment: Qualify until the SpecLFB run is re-scored: the counted tests were speculative cache hits by the second speculative load, not first-load installs.
proposed: and exposing the mechanism of SpecLFB's known unprotected-first-load bug in [N] tests
evidence: see the results.tex 68/300 note; PAPER_RESULTS.md:302-304; hooks_speclfb_and_uv6.md

anchor: it actually \textbf{obtained data} --- either it \emph{reached the cache} or it received a \emph{store-to-load forward}.
comment: This is the delay-defense criterion (STT, ReCon, SPT: the tainted transmitter must not execute). For InvisiSpec, SpecLFB and CleanupSpec a speculative load may obtain data (into the SB or LFB, or install and be cleaned); their criterion is a footprint (fill, evict, coherence or replacement change, or un-undone install) by any unsafe speculative load in the protected structures. The memaccess and expose ticks named earlier are not what those criteria use (expose is an allowed event in invisispec.json).
proposed: Split the bullet: delay defenses (STT, ReCon, SPT) use the data-obtained gate on the transmitter; hide/undo defenses (InvisiSpec, SpecLFB, CleanupSpec) use a per-defense footprint criterion over the cache-event hook lines (Table~\ref{tab:xmitcriteria}).
evidence: STT §6.1 p5; InvisiSpec §V-A p4; SpecLFB §6.1 p637, §9 p643; CleanupSpec §1 p2; specs/leakage/{invisispec,speclfb,cleanupspec}.json

anchor: Given a target transmitter defined by our leakage backbone, we must specify how to detect transmission.
comment: For the three footprint defenses detection is not tied to the target transmitter: check_footprint never reads the transmitter PC and counts any squashed instruction younger than lc, so the Alloy model only chooses the stimulus there.
proposed: For delay defenses the predicate is evaluated on the target transmitter; for footprint defenses it covers every unsafe speculative load, and the target transmitter is reported for attribution.

anchor: SpecLFB, InvisiSpec and CleanupSpec currently reuse STT's model; note the per-defense exceptions in the shared skeleton.
comment: State what reuse costs: STT_6 protects only speculatively accessed data (AMuLeT's ARCH-SEQ), while all three protect every unsafe speculative load (CT-SEQ; CleanupSpec names register and computed secrets), and STT_6 realizes only control-flow squashes while InvisiSpec-Futuristic, CleanupSpec and SpecLFB also cover other squash sources. STT_6 is a sound but incomplete stimulus, and the footprint verdict does not use its protection set.
evidence: AMuLeT §3.1 p5, p8; CleanupSpec §2.1 p3; InvisiSpec §IV-A1 p4; SpecLFB §5 p637-638; simspect wiki/design/MODELS_AND_BUILDS.md PART 7

comment: 'All memory' with no update rule is a CT-style set that STT does not protect; STT_6 also removes memory read by a load with no older unresolved branch (untaint at the visibility point), and STT puts attacks on non-speculatively accessed data out of scope.
proposed: All memory, minus memory read by a load with no older unresolved branch (STT untaints an access instruction's output once it is safe)
evidence: STT §3 Fig. 3 p3, §6.1 p5; simspect STAGE1_alloy/models/STT_6.als:326-332

anchor: STT and Recon still use the generic load gate.
comment: This reads as a gap, but the transmitter-keyed gate is the right shape for delay defenses: STT lets untainted speculative loads execute and change the cache, so a footprint criterion would flag the access load. The criteria are also written down now (specs/leakage/stt.json, recon.json), though no checker reads them.
proposed: STT and ReCon use the transmitter-keyed load gate by design, since they delay only tainted transmitters.

anchor: observes and outside its dataflow stimulus.
comment: UV6 as published leaks a secret register with a single speculative load, i.e. non-speculatively accessed data, which STT and so STT_6 do not protect (that is why AMuLeT tests STT under ARCH-SEQ and SpecLFB under CT-SEQ). SimSpect's UV6 hits are on the second speculative load (the model's transmitter), which a 2026-10-28 code read attributes to a head-skip implementation artifact rather than the first-load rule.
proposed: Say that UV6's mechanism (an unprotected unsafe load) is visible to SimSpect, but its published form, a register secret leaked by the first speculative load, lies outside STT_6's protection set.
evidence: AMuLeT p3 ('leaking secret registers with a single speculative load'), §3.1 p5 (CT-SEQ vs ARCH-SEQ); STT §3 Fig. 3 p3; simspect wiki/findings/audits/2026-10-28/hooks_speclfb_and_uv6.md:13-21
